passage_text: Researchers at the University of Midvale conducted a controlled laboratory study to investigate the impact of acute sleep deprivation on memory consolidation in adult male mice. The experiment involved three groups: a control group that was allowed 12 hours of uninterrupted sleep, a group subjected to 4 hours of sleep deprivation, and a group subjected to 8 hours of sleep deprivation. After the sleep manipulation, all mice were tested on a novel object recognition task, a widely used behavioral assay for assessing recognition memory. The mean recognition index (percentage of time spent exploring the novel object) for each group was recorded along with the standard deviation. The researchers hypothesized that increasing duration of sleep deprivation would lead to a progressive decline in memory performance, thereby providing evidence for the role of sleep in memory consolidation processes.
table_data:
| Sleep Condition | Mean Recognition Index (%) | Standard Deviation |
|-----------------|----------------------------|--------------------|
| Control (12h)   | 85.2                       | 4.3                |
| 4h Deprivation  | 72.5                       | 5.1                |
| 8h Deprivation  | 60.1                       | 6.0                |
stem: Based on the data presented in the table, which of the following best describes the effect of sleep deprivation on memory performance in the mice?

options.B: Sleep deprivation has no effect on memory performance.
options.D: Sleep deprivation improves memory performance only at 4 hours.

explanation: The recognition index decreases from 85.2% in the control group to 72.5% after 4 hours of deprivation and further to 60.1% after 8 hours, indicating a progressive decline in memory performance with increased sleep deprivation.
trap: Reading the recognition index as an error measure, so that the lower values after deprivation would seem to mean better memory.

stem: If the researchers wanted to test whether caffeine administration could mitigate the negative effects of sleep deprivation on memory, which experimental design would be most appropriate?

options.A: Randomized controlled trial with caffeine vs. placebo groups within each sleep deprivation level.
options.B: Observational cohort study tracking caffeine consumption in mice.
options.C: Cross‑sectional survey of caffeine use among laboratory staff.
options.D: Case‑control study comparing caffeine‑treated and untreated mice after deprivation.

explanation: A randomized controlled trial allows for direct comparison of caffeine versus placebo within each deprivation condition, controlling for confounding variables and establishing causality.
trap: Choosing the case-control option because it compares caffeine-treated and untreated mice, although a case-control design selects subjects by outcome and lacks random assignment.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: Mean recognition index declined progressively from the control group to the 4-hour group to the 8-hour group.
options.B: The 8-hour deprivation group scored 25.1 percentage points lower than the control group.
options.C: The 4-hour and 8-hour deprivation groups differed in mean recognition index by 12.4 percentage points.
options.D: Sleep deprivation also impaired recognition memory in female mice.

explanation: Correct: D. The study used adult male mice only, so nothing can be concluded for female mice. Why the others are wrong: A) The means are 85.2, 72.5 and 60.1, a progressive decline. B) 85.2 - 60.1 = 25.1. C) 72.5 - 60.1 = 12.4.
trap: Extending results from male mice to both sexes.

explanation: Correct: A. (85.2 - 60.1)/85.2 x 100 = 25.1/85.2 x 100 = 29.5%. Why the others are wrong: B) 25.1 is the absolute difference in percentage points, not a percent decrease. trap: Dividing by the deprived-group value or reporting the absolute difference as a percent.
